title: Chapter 10 – The Patient Man
html:
[Zhao Family of Red Ridge – Patriarch Zhao Heng]

The pine is two hundred and twelve years old, and Zhao Heng has been shaping it for a hundred and forty of them.

It stands on a low table of black lacquer in the courtyard of his private house at the top of Red Ridge, in a shallow glazed dish no wider than a man's two hands. It is no taller than his forearm. Its trunk twists twice upon itself, like a dragon turning in its sleep, and its branches lie in three flat tiers of dark green needles, each one as precise as a brushstroke. Visitors from the Sect who have seen it have asked him what he would take for it. He has never named a price.

Every morning he trims it. Not much. A single needle. Two. A bud that is growing a little too eagerly toward the light. He uses a pair of silver scissors no longer than his little finger, and he takes his time, and when he is done he sits back on his heels and looks at it for a while before he goes in to breakfast.

His grandsons find this tedious. Zhao Qian, who is fourteen and at the seventh layer of Qi Refining and has the patience of a struck match, once asked him why he did not simply cut the tree into the shape he wanted and be done with it.

"Because then it would die," Zhao Heng told him. "A branch cut too hard bleeds. A branch bent too fast snaps." He snipped a single needle. "But a branch bent a little every day, for long enough, will hold any shape you like. And after a hundred years," he set down the scissors, "it will believe it grew that way."

Zhao Qian had not understood. Zhao Heng had not expected him to.

This morning, four days after the Lin tribute, he trims two needles from the lowest tier, and sits back, and thinks about Green Pine Hill.

Then he goes out into the training yard, as he does every morning, and practices.

The yard is paved with slabs of the red ridge stone, worn smooth by a century of feet. Zhao Heng stands in the center of it in his plain morning robe, and breathes once, and the Qi of the second-grade vein under Red Ridge rises up through the paving and into him like water up a wick.

He does not make hand seals. He has not needed them for a hundred years. He simply looks at the far end of the yard, where a row of iron practice posts stands against the wall, and thinks of a shape.

The paving stones at his feet crack. A dozen shards the size of arrowheads lift out of them, rust-red and razor-edged, and hang in the air around him, turning slowly, as if they are listening. Black Iron Array. A Yellow-grade earth art, built for the Foundation. Then they are gone, and there is a sound like hail on a roof, and twelve of the iron posts at the end of the yard each have a shard driven through them to the stone behind.

He looks at the thirteenth post, the one he did not choose, and makes a small gesture with two fingers, palm down.

The air above the post grows heavy. The post bends. Not breaks: bends, slowly, groaning, as if a great invisible hand is pressing down on it from above, until its top is touching the paving at its own foot. Quaking Mountain Lance. A man standing under that would not bend. He would fold.

Zhao Heng straightens his sleeves. At his belt, the little bronze incense burner his father gave him on the day he reached the Foundation breathes a thin thread of gray smoke that smells of nothing at all. Profound grade, from a Sect furnace, worth more than the whole Lin treasury. It does one thing. It folds a cultivator's aura in on itself, so that a man at the late stage of Foundation Establishment can walk into a room full of Qi Refining cultivators and press on them no harder than a steward. He wears it everywhere. It is a great deal easier to be underestimated than to be feared.

He looks up at the top of the wall, thirty feet above the yard. He steps onto nothing. A slim gray blade the length of his arm slides out from his sleeve and under his feet, and the air beneath it hardens, and he rises, unhurried, as if climbing a stair, and steps off onto the parapet.

From there he can see east, two valleys away, a low green hill under a faint haze of morning smoke.

He looks at it for a long time.

\ \ \*

Red Ridge is a long spur of rust-colored rock two valleys west of the Lin hill, stained red by the iron in its stone, with a second-grade spirit vein beneath it that hums like a beehive. His grandfather took it a hundred and forty years ago, a rogue cultivator with three sons and a sword, from a family of herb farmers who did not argue for long. His father built the walls. Zhao Heng built everything else.

He reached Foundation Establishment at sixty-one, the first of his line. That was a hundred and twenty-four years ago. In the century since, he has turned a hill fort with nine cultivators into a family of forty, with shops in every county town within a day's ride, three spirit-rice estates, a share in the Willow Ford salt trade and a seat in the outer court of the Azure Cloud Sect. He has done most of it without drawing a sword.

He is a hundred and eighty-five. He has been at the late stage of Foundation Establishment for thirty years.

That is the thing he thinks about, in the mornings, after the pine.

A Foundation Establishment cultivator lives about two hundred and fifty years. Zhao Heng has perhaps sixty-five left. The Foundation has four stages, early, middle, late and peak, and the climb between them is slow and steep, and the climb past the peak is steeper still. Beyond it lies Purple Mansion: the realm in which a cultivator's foundation opens like a flower into an inner mansion of the spirit, and from that mansion, for the first time, comes a divine ability of his own, something no technique can teach and no enemy can copy. Another century of life. And a seat not in the outer court of the Azure Cloud Sect, but in the inner.

A second-grade vein will not carry a man there. He has tried. His foundation sits at the late stage like a cart wheel in a rut, full and polished and going nowhere.

He needs something more. And he knows exactly where it is.

\ \ \*

He was nine when his grandfather told him.

The old man was dying, slowly, of an old wound that had never healed, and in the last month of his life he took his grandson up onto the wall of Red Ridge and pointed east, toward the green hill two valleys away.

"I fought Lin Shoucheng for that hill for two years," he said. "I lost two brothers on it. In the end I settled for this." He waved a hand at the rust-red rock. "Do you know why I wanted it so badly?"

Zhao Heng had shaken his head.

"Because Lin Shoucheng found something under it." The old man's voice dropped. "I went there once as a guest, after the fighting stopped. He was very polite. He showed me the hall and the terraces and the chamber where he cultivated. Forty steps down." He laughed, a dry rattle. "He took me to the top of the steps, and no farther. But I stood at the top of those steps, boy, and I felt it. Underneath the vein. Something old. Older than any clan in this province. Older than the Sect." He gripped his grandson's shoulder with fingers like iron hooks. "Lin Shoucheng was a rogue with a three-element root and no master, and he reached Foundation Establishment in under ten years sitting on that hill. You don't do that with a first-grade vein. The vein is nothing. The vein is only what leaks out from behind the door."

"What door?" Zhao Heng had asked.

But the old man had only looked east, and said nothing else, and died a month later.

Zhao Heng has thought about that door for a hundred and seventy-six years.

He knows a little more now than he did at nine. He has paid travelers who once worked on the hill to describe the chamber. He has asked his steward, over the years, a great many careful questions. The Lins themselves, as far as he can tell, have forgotten it entirely. The founder died a hundred and seven years ago. His son never mentioned it. His grandson, Lin Zhenshan, sits on the cushion at the bottom of the forty steps every morning and cultivates on the vein and has never once, so far as anyone can tell, looked behind him.

When Lin Zhenshan dies, the hill will fall. The Lins have no Foundation and no one who will reach it. And when the hill falls, Zhao Heng will walk down the forty steps and find out what Lin Shoucheng found.

That is the plan. It has been the plan for fifty years. And the Compact, which forbids him so much, has even given him a way to make it lawful when the time comes. It has a clause that every elder in the outer court knows and none of them names aloud: when a tributary patriarch dies without a confirmed heir, a neighboring elder holding a petition from a member of that family may enter the house to keep order for three days, until the Sect confirms a successor. Three days. With the right petition, signed by the right member of the family, a man could do a great deal in three days.

Zhao Heng already owns the member of the family. He only needs the old man to die.

The difficulty is that he cannot simply kill the old man and take the hill.

\ \ \*

He could. That is the irony that sometimes makes him smile, in the mornings, with the silver scissors in his hand. On any day he chose, he could walk up to the Lin gate and kill Lin Zhenshan in twenty exchanges, and his ninth-layer sons with him, and there is no one on that hill who could stop him.

And the next day, the Azure Cloud Sect's Enforcement Hall would come to Red Ridge.

The Vassal Compact is older than the Zhao family. It is very simple. The Sect takes tribute from a hundred families in the outer counties, and in exchange, it does not let them eat one another. A tributary family that raises its hand against another loses its trade rights, its seat in the outer court, its standing in every market the Sect controls. A Foundation Establishment elder who kills a tributary patriarch loses more than that. Zhao Heng has seen it happen once, sixty years ago, to a family on the southern border who thought the Sect was too far away to notice. The Enforcement Hall noticed. There is a lake there now where their hill used to be.

But that is not even the real reason.

The real reason is that if the Enforcement Hall comes to Green Pine Hill to investigate a murdered patriarch, the Enforcement Hall will walk through every room on that hill. And sooner or later, someone with a Golden Core and a great deal of curiosity will walk down forty steps, and stand where his grandfather stood, and feel what his grandfather felt.

And then it will not be the Zhao family that opens the door.

So the hill must fall by itself. Quietly. Lawfully. The way a branch bends.

\ \ \*

He has been bending it for a long time.

He undercuts the Lin talismans in every market, at a loss he can afford and they cannot. He offers to lease their terraces, knowing they will refuse, so that every year the refusal costs them a little more. He sends gifts on every birth and condolences on every death. He asked for the trade levy at the Outer Affairs Hall himself, the moment his steward told him the Lin shop's income was rising; the outer court found it reasonable, because the outer court finds most things reasonable when a family with a seat proposes them.

And he owns Lin Wenhai.

He bought Lin Wenhai eleven years ago, in a gambling house in the eastern quarter of Willow Ford called the Pavilion of Nine Dice. Wenhai had lost four hundred stones there in a single night, money he did not have, to men who did not forgive debts. Zhao Heng bought the debt for two hundred and sent his steward to tell Wenhai who owned it now.

Since then, Wenhai has paid the interest the only way he can: by stealing from his own family's shop, ten stones a season, then fifty, and by reporting. Every council. Every tribute. Every breakthrough among the young cultivators, and every cough from the old man. It was Wenhai who told him the tribute was thirty stones short, five years ago, and Zhao Heng still remembers the expression on Lin Zhenshan's face when he said the number aloud over the teacups. Like a man who has stepped on a stair that is not there.

Wenhai is careful. Zhao Heng made sure of that. On the second year, he gave him a box: a small, plain box of white jade, Mortal grade, the kind a merchant keeps his seals in. It is lined inside with a formation no larger than a coin that turns away ordinary spiritual sense like a mirror turns away light. Every letter Zhao Heng sends goes into that box. Every stone Wenhai takes goes into that box. Lin Zhenshan could stand in the same room with it and sweep his sense across it for an hour and feel nothing but jade.

The Compact requires proof. The box makes sure there will never be any.

\ \ \*

What troubles him this morning is the paper.

The Lin shop in Willow Ford is selling out within two days of each delivery. The Zhao shop across the square, which has undersold the Lins for forty years, sold nine talismans last month. Nine. His steward reports that the Lin Mirror Guards hold for a minute, and the farmers call them miracle charms, and the Sect's Talisman Pavilion has given the family a contract.

And all of it, apparently, comes from a one-armed smith.

Zhao Heng, on his wall, thinks about that.

Fifteen years ago, when he was newly seated in the outer court, he heard a story from an elder of the Coral Tide Sect at a banquet in the provincial capital. There had been an artificer on some nameless island east of the Coral Gate, the elder said, a weapon-smith so good that certain people, people one did not name at banquets, had paid him for years to make blades for them. Then the smith had refused to make any more. Those people had come to his workshop to change his mind. They had cut off his right arm. That night the workshop burned, and someone pulled the smith out of the fire, and he vanished.

A one-armed smith from the islands. On Green Pine Hill.

Zhao Heng does not believe in coincidences. He believes in patterns. And a pattern is forming on Green Pine Hill that he does not like: the paper, the smith, the talisman contract, the rising income. The Lins are not dying as fast as they should. They are getting stronger.

The branch is bending back.

\ \ \*

Zhao Qian finds him on the wall at noon.

The boy comes up the steps two at a time, a saber at his hip and his face flushed. He is tall for fourteen, lean and sharp-featured, with his grandmother's high cheekbones and none of her sense. Six years ago his root cracked two of the crystals on the Zhao family stele: metal and fire, both nearly pure, the best root born on Red Ridge in three generations. He has been told so all his life. It shows.

"Grandfather. They say the Lin shop's paper comes from the smith." He stops at the parapet. "The one-armed islander. Let me go over there. I'll test him. A smith who drinks all day can't still be at the ninth layer, whatever they say. I'll break his arm. His other one."

Zhao Heng does not turn from the view.

"And when you have broken it," he says, "and the Lin Patriarch writes to the Outer Affairs Hall that the heir of the Zhao family crossed the boundary of a tributary house and maimed a guest elder under its protection, what then?"

Zhao Qian opens his mouth, and closes it.

"You will be called before the Hall," says Zhao Heng. "Our seat in the outer court will be suspended while they deliberate. Our trade rights in Willow Ford will be suspended. The Lins will receive compensation, out of our treasury, and the Sect will take a tenth for its trouble." He finally looks at his grandson. "And every family in the outer counties will learn that the Zhao of Red Ridge cannot keep their children on a leash. Is that what you want?"

"No, Grandfather."

"Then go back to your saber. Practice the Silent Horizon until you can cut a falling leaf in four pieces at ten paces. You are at the seventh layer, Qian, and the Lin boy with the triple root is at the fifth, and in five years he will catch you if you spend your mornings thinking about one-armed smiths." He turns back to the view. "We do not break things on Green Pine Hill. We wait for them to break."

The boy goes. Zhao Heng hears his boots on the steps, hard and angry, and sighs.

Patience, like a pine, cannot be taught to a child. It can only be grown.

\ \ \*

Lin Wenhai comes to the Pavilion of Nine Dice on the fifth night, as instructed.

He comes up the back stair, as always, with his hood up and his hands in his sleeves, and sits down at the table in the small private room where Zhao Heng is waiting with a pot of tea and the door closed. He does not drink the tea. He never does. His soft hands are restless on the table.

"Patriarch," he says.

"Steward." Zhao Heng pours. "Tell me about the arbiter."

Wenhai tells him. The old man has been in the library every night since the tribute. He is searching for the deed. Lin Shoucheng's land deed, registered with the county magistrate at Willow Ford a hundred and fifty years ago, with a map of the boundaries and the spring and the channel drawn on it in the founder's own hand, and the magistrate's seal at the bottom. It is in a lacquered tube with a brass cap, on the second shelf of the library, where it has always been. The old man has not found it yet because he is looking for a second copy. He knows where the first one is.

"A deed," says Zhao Heng, "with the spring on it."

"Yes, Patriarch."

"Then the arbiter will rule for the Lins."

Wenhai licks his lips. "Yes, Patriarch. Almost certainly. Unless—"

"Unless the deed is lost."

The steward goes very still.

"It is an old library," says Zhao Heng mildly. "Old roof. Old shelves. Winter is coming. Roofs leak. Lamps tip over. Paper rots." He sips his tea. "It would be a great pity if the deed were lost. And if, in the same accident, the account books on the bottom shelf were ruined too, ten years of them, that would be an even greater pity. For your father. Not, perhaps, for you."

Wenhai's face has gone the color of old tallow. His hands have stopped moving.

"Your father has been in that library every night," Zhao Heng says. "He has been reading your account books, Steward. Not the deed. Your books." He sets down his cup. "How long, do you think, before he reads them carefully enough?"

There is a long silence.

"The roof," Wenhai says at last, hoarsely. "It would have to be the roof. A storm. If the tiles were loose."

"Winter storms are very common," says Zhao Heng.

"And the deed itself? If it is merely damp, he will dry it and take it to the arbiter anyway."

"Then it should not be merely damp. It should be gone." Zhao Heng smiles. "Bring it to me, Steward. I will keep it safe. Somewhere very dry."

Wenhai stares at the tabletop for a long time. Then he nods. Once. Jerkily. Like a puppet with a cut string.

"Good," says Zhao Heng. "And the smith. Tell me about the smith."

Wenhai tells him, haltingly. The smith refused the forty stones. Threw the steward out of his forge into the courtyard in the middle of the night and threatened to pour Cloud Mist Peach Wine down his neck. He drinks with the old man every evening on the bench outside the main hall. He takes no stipend. He makes paper and hoes and teaches no one but the pseudo-root boy. He keeps an iron rod by his bed.

"An iron rod," says Zhao Heng.

"Spirit iron, I think. He uses it to stir the forge." Wenhai hesitates. "He doesn't look like much, Patriarch. A drunk with one arm."

"Neither does a coiled snake," says Zhao Heng, "until you put your foot on it." He refills his own cup. "Leave him alone. Don't offer him anything else. Don't go near his forge at night. If he is who I think he is, there are people far less patient than I am who have been looking for him for fifteen years."

Wenhai's face shows that he does not understand. Zhao Heng does not explain.

\ \ \*

When the steward has gone, Zhao Heng stays in the small room a while, alone, with the cold tea.

He did not tell Wenhai about the door. He has never told Wenhai about the door. A steward who knows what his master truly wants is a steward who can sell it to someone else.

He thinks about the smith, and the paper, and the Lin boy with the pseudo-root whom Wenhai mentioned in passing, the one who follows the smith around like a puppy and carries his gravel. He dismisses the boy. A pseudo-root of seven or eight, struggling to hold the first layer, is not worth a thought.

He thinks about the old man in the library, reading account books by lamplight.

And he thinks, briefly, about the other thing his steward mentioned, the thing the farmers have been whispering about in Willow Ford market for a week. Three animals found in the outer forest east of the river, below the Lin terraces. A wolf. Two deer. Drained of blood, all three of them, with two small round burns on their throats.

Zhao Heng has been a cultivator for a hundred and seventy years. He knows what kind of thing drains a wolf of blood and leaves a burn the size of a thumb.

He thinks about it for a while, turning his cup slowly in his fingers. Then he sets it down.

The Compact forbids the Zhao family to harm the Lins. It says nothing at all about what the Beast Mountains might do to them.

"Let the Lins worry about it," he says, to the empty room, and goes home to his pine.
